questions.stem: What was the aim of Harlow's 1958 study with infant rhesus monkeys?
options: To measure how quickly monkeys learn to use simple tools
To test whether attachment depends more on feeding or on comfort
To test whether monkeys could learn to recognise their own mother
To find the critical period for language in young monkeys
questions.explanation: Harlow tested the popular view that infants attach to whoever feeds them, by asking whether feeding or comfort mattered more. His study had nothing to do with language or tool use.

questions.stem: In Harlow's study, infant monkeys separated from their mothers were given two surrogate mothers. What were they?
options: Two wire models, only one of which gave milk
One made of bare wire and one covered in soft cloth
One real adult monkey and one model made of wire
Two cloth-covered models, only one of which moved
questions.explanation: The infants were raised with a bare wire surrogate and a soft cloth-covered surrogate, and either one could be fitted with a milk bottle. Comparing them separated the effect of feeding from the effect of comfort.

questions.stem: Which finding from Harlow's study is correct?
options: Infants spent most of their time on whichever mother gave milk, whether it was wire or cloth
Infants spent equal time on each mother, regardless of which one of them gave milk
Infants clung to the wire mother, because it was easier to grip than cloth
Infants spent most of their time on the cloth mother, even if only the wire one gave milk
questions.explanation: The infants clung to the cloth mother for most of the day and went to the wire mother only briefly to feed. This showed that comfort, not food, was the main basis of their attachment.

questions.stem: When a noisy mechanical toy was placed in their cage, Harlow's infant monkeys ran to the cloth mother. What does this suggest?
options: The cloth mother gave a sense of security and comfort
The cloth mother was the only one that gave them milk
The infants could not tell the two surrogates apart
The wire mother had frightened them more than the toy
questions.explanation: Running to the cloth mother when frightened shows she was a source of security, much as a real mother is. This happened even for infants who were fed by the wire mother.

questions.stem: What was the main contribution of Harlow's study to psychology?
options: It proved that monkeys and humans attach in identical ways
It showed contact comfort, not just feeding, is central to attachment
It showed that attachment forms only to the caregiver who feeds the infant
It identified three types of attachment in human infants
questions.explanation: Harlow's work challenged the idea that infants attach to whoever feeds them and highlighted the importance of contact comfort. The three attachment types came from Ainsworth's research with human infants.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of Harlow's study?
options: It used too many monkeys for the results to be analysed accurately
It found that feeding is the basis of attachment, a view later disproved
The monkeys suffered lasting distress and social harm, raising serious ethical concerns
The cloth and wire mothers both gave milk the whole time, so feeding was never really tested
questions.explanation: Separating infant monkeys from their mothers caused distress, and those raised with surrogates later showed social difficulties, so the research is criticised on ethical grounds. Harlow controlled which mother gave milk, which is how feeding was tested.

questions.stem: A student argues that Harlow's findings prove human babies need physical contact more than food. What is the best evaluation of this claim?
options: It is wrong, because Harlow found the monkeys preferred the mother that gave milk
It is fully supported, because Harlow also tested human infants in the same way
It overstates the findings, because results from monkeys may not apply directly to humans
It is fully supported, because rhesus monkeys and humans develop in exactly identical ways
questions.explanation: Rhesus monkeys share many features with humans, but generalising animal findings to people must be done with caution. Harlow found the opposite of a milk preference, and he did not test human infants.

questions.stem: Bowlby defined attachment as:
options: a temporary preference for whoever feeds the infant
a learned habit of seeking food from one caregiver
an inborn fear of strangers that appears at birth
a lasting psychological connectedness between human beings
questions.explanation: Bowlby described attachment as a lasting psychological connectedness between people, an emotional bond rather than a link to whoever provides food.

questions.stem: Bowlby's evolutionary perspective proposes that attachment:
options: is innate and evolved because staying near a caregiver helps infants survive
is learned when infants come to link their caregiver with the pleasure of being fed
develops only after a child has learned to speak and walk
is a cultural habit that differs completely between societies
questions.explanation: Bowlby argued that attachment is an innate, adaptive system: infants who stayed close to a caregiver were more likely to survive. Linking the caregiver with food is the learning view Bowlby rejected.

questions.stem: According to Bowlby, why do young infants smile, cry and cling?
options: These innate behaviours bring caregivers close and help the infant survive
They are learned only after the infant is rewarded with food
They show that the infant has already formed several equal attachments
They are signs that the critical period for attachment has ended
questions.explanation: Bowlby saw smiling, crying and clinging as inborn behaviours that draw caregivers near and keep them close, increasing the infant's chance of survival. He did not see them as learned through feeding.

questions.stem: In Bowlby's theory, monotropy is:
options: the time after which no attachment can form at all
the mental template of relationships formed in infancy
the tendency to form one primary attachment that is more important than others
the tendency to form equally strong attachments with everyone who cares for the infant
questions.explanation: Monotropy is Bowlby's idea that infants form one special, primary attachment, usually to the mother, that is more important than any other. The mental template of relationships is the internal working model.

questions.stem: Bowlby originally proposed a critical period for attachment. According to this idea, if no attachment forms in the first few years:
options: the child will attach only to the person who feeds them
the child will form a secure attachment with a stranger
later attachments will be very difficult or impossible to form
the child will form attachments more easily once they are older
questions.explanation: Bowlby believed attachment must form within a critical period in the first few years of life or it might never form properly. The later idea of a sensitive period softened this claim.

questions.stem: How does a sensitive period differ from a critical period?
options: A sensitive period applies to animals, while a critical period applies to humans
Attachment forms most easily in a sensitive period but can still form later
Attachment can form only during a sensitive period and never after it
A sensitive period happens before birth, while a critical period comes after
questions.explanation: A sensitive period is the time when attachment forms most easily, but it can still form afterwards with more difficulty. A critical period implies a strict window after which it cannot form at all.

questions.stem: Bowlby's maternal deprivation hypothesis predicts that a child who is separated from the primary attachment figure for long periods in the first few years will:
options: be more likely to have lasting emotional and social difficulties
form stronger attachments as a result of the separation
be unaffected, as long as all of the child's physical needs are met
develop more advanced language than other children
questions.explanation: Bowlby argued that disruption of the primary attachment during the critical period could cause long-term emotional, social and cognitive problems. He did not believe meeting physical needs alone was enough.

questions.stem: Which finding would most challenge Bowlby's maternal deprivation hypothesis?
options: Infants who strongly prefer their mother to unfamiliar adults by the end of the first year
Children separated early who form healthy relationships after good alternative care
Children separated early from their mothers who later show emotional difficulties as adolescents
Infants who become upset when their mother leaves the room and calm on her return
questions.explanation: If children who experience early separation develop normally given good alternative care, the separation itself did not cause lasting harm, which challenges the hypothesis. Later emotional difficulties after separation would support it.

questions.stem: Bowlby's internal working model is:
options: the tendency to form one primary attachment that matters more than all others
a mental template of self, others and relationships formed from early attachment
a laboratory procedure for observing and classifying attachment in infants
the period early in life when an attachment forms most easily and quickly
questions.explanation: The internal working model is a mental template, based on the early attachment relationship, that shapes expectations about oneself, other people and future relationships. The laboratory method for measuring attachment is Ainsworth's Strange Situation.

questions.stem: Mira's parents responded warmly and reliably to her as a baby. As an adult, she expects her partners to be trustworthy and supportive. Which part of Bowlby's theory explains this?
options: Monotropy
The critical period
Maternal deprivation
The internal working model
questions.explanation: Bowlby proposed that the early attachment relationship forms an internal working model that guides expectations in later relationships. A reliable early caregiver leads to expectations that others will be trustworthy.

questions.stem: Research shows that many infants form several attachments at once, to fathers, grandparents and siblings, as well as mothers. Which part of Bowlby's theory does this most directly challenge?
options: The internal working model
The evolutionary perspective
The definition of attachment
Monotropy
questions.explanation: Monotropy claims one primary attachment is special and more important than the rest, so evidence of several equally important attachments challenges it. Forming attachments at all is consistent with the evolutionary perspective.

questions.stem: Which real-world change is linked to Bowlby's work on attachment?
options: Hospitals separating newborns from parents to prevent infection
Hospitals allowing parents to stay with young children during treatment
Schools grouping children by age so they meet the critical period
Child care centres feeding infants on a fixed timetable to build attachment
questions.explanation: Bowlby's emphasis on the harm of separation helped change hospital practice, so parents could stay with young children rather than visit briefly. Separating children from parents runs against his recommendations.

questions.stem: What was the aim of Ainsworth's Strange Situation?
options: To measure the type of attachment between an infant and caregiver
To measure how quickly infants develop object permanence
To test whether infants prefer cloth or wire surrogate mothers
To find out whether attachment differs between countries
questions.explanation: Ainsworth designed the Strange Situation as a standardised way of observing and classifying the quality of attachment between infants, aged around one year, and their mothers. Comparing countries was the aim of van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's later analysis.

questions.stem: In the Strange Situation, an infant is observed:
options: at home over several months while the mother keeps a detailed diary of feeding times
while choosing between a soft cloth surrogate mother and a wire one that gives milk
through short episodes in which the mother leaves and returns and a stranger comes and goes
alone in a playroom for an hour while researchers record how often the infant cries
questions.explanation: The procedure is a sequence of brief episodes in a playroom in which the mother leaves and returns and a stranger enters and leaves, while the infant is observed. Choosing between surrogates describes Harlow's monkey study.

questions.stem: Which behaviour was a key measure in the Strange Situation?
options: Whether the infant could find a toy hidden under a cushion
How much milk the infant drank during the session
How the infant responded when reunited with the mother
How quickly the infant learned to walk across the room
questions.explanation: Ainsworth recorded separation anxiety, stranger anxiety, willingness to explore and, especially, the infant's behaviour on reunion with the mother. Searching for a hidden toy tests object permanence.

questions.stem: Which description fits a Type B, securely attached infant in the Strange Situation?
options: Explores little, is extremely distressed when the mother leaves and then resists her comfort on her return
Explores only with the stranger, and shows equal distress whether the mother or the stranger leaves
Explores using the mother as a safe base, is upset when she leaves and is quickly comforted on her return
Explores freely, shows little distress when the mother leaves and then ignores her on her return
questions.explanation: Securely attached infants use the mother as a safe base for exploring, show some distress at separation and are easily comforted when she returns. Little distress and ignoring the mother describes insecure avoidant attachment.

questions.stem: An infant who shows little distress when the mother leaves, treats the stranger much like the mother, and avoids the mother when she returns is classified as:
options: Type A, insecure avoidant
Type B, secure
Type C, insecure resistant
Type B, insecure avoidant
questions.explanation: Little separation distress and avoiding the mother on reunion are the features of Type A, insecure avoidant attachment. Type B is secure attachment, so it cannot also be insecure avoidant.

questions.stem: Fourteen-month-old Noah explores little, is very distressed when his mother leaves, and on her return reaches to be picked up, then pushes her away angrily. His attachment type is:
options: Type A, secure
Type C, insecure resistant
Type A, insecure avoidant
Type B, secure
questions.explanation: Clinginess, intense distress at separation and seeking but then resisting comfort on reunion are the features of Type C, insecure resistant attachment. An avoidant infant shows little distress and ignores the mother.

questions.stem: In Ainsworth's sample, which attachment type was the most common?
options: Type A, insecure avoidant
Type C, insecure resistant
All three were equally common
Type B, secure
questions.explanation: Most infants in Ainsworth's sample were securely attached, with smaller numbers classed as insecure avoidant or insecure resistant.

questions.stem: What is a key contribution of the Strange Situation to psychology?
options: It showed that attachment types are identical in every culture
It showed that attachment forms only after the second birthday
It gave researchers a standardised, repeatable way to classify attachment
It proved that attachment depends on which caregiver feeds the infant
questions.explanation: The Strange Situation's standardised procedure meant attachment could be measured the same way by different researchers and in different countries. It did not show attachment depends on feeding, and later studies found variation between cultures.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of Ainsworth's Strange Situation?
options: It relied entirely on mothers' written reports of how their infants behaved at home
It was carried out with rhesus monkeys, so it may not apply to humans
It was so unstructured that no two researchers ran it the same way
Its sample was American families, so its categories may not suit other cultures
questions.explanation: The Strange Situation was developed with American families, and behaviour judged insecure in one culture may reflect different child-rearing norms in another. It was a standardised observation of human infants, not a report or an animal study.

questions.stem: What kind of research did van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) carry out?
options: A case study of a child raised in severe isolation
A meta-analysis of Strange Situation studies from eight countries
A longitudinal study following one group of infants into adulthood
An experiment comparing cloth and wire surrogate mothers
questions.explanation: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg combined the results of 32 Strange Situation studies from eight countries in a meta-analysis. The cloth and wire surrogates belong to Harlow's study.

questions.stem: What did van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg find about secure attachment?
options: It was less common than avoidant attachment overall
It was found in equal numbers to the other two types
It was the most common type in every country studied
It was the most common type only in the United States
questions.explanation: Secure attachment was the most common type in all the countries in the analysis, which suggests it may be the norm across cultures. The proportions of the insecure types varied more.

questions.stem: In van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's analysis, which pattern was found?
options: Resistant attachment was relatively common in West Germany; avoidant was relatively common in Japan and Israel
Avoidant attachment was the most common type in Japan and Israel, ahead of secure attachment
Resistant and avoidant attachment occurred at exactly the same rate in every country
Avoidant attachment was relatively common in West Germany; resistant was relatively common in Japan and Israel
questions.explanation: Avoidant attachment was relatively more common in West Germany, while resistant attachment was relatively more common in Japan and Israel. Secure attachment was still the most common type in each of these countries.

questions.stem: Which finding from van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg warns against describing a whole country as having one typical attachment pattern?
options: Secure attachment was the most common type in every country studied
The Strange Situation was used in all of the studies they analysed
Some countries contributed many more studies to the analysis than others did
The variation within countries was greater than the variation between them
questions.explanation: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg found that variation within countries was about one and a half times the variation between countries, so differences among groups inside a country can be larger than differences between countries. Secure attachment being most common does not address within-country variation.

questions.stem: Which is the most likely effect of an enriched early environment, with plenty of stimulation and social interaction, on the developing brain?
options: A smaller amygdala and reduced emotional responses
More complex neural connections, such as more dendritic branching
Faster proliferation of neurons after adolescence has ended
Earlier completion of myelination in the whole of the pre-frontal cortex
questions.explanation: Stimulating, socially rich environments are linked with more complex neural connections, including more dendritic branching and synapses. Proliferation happens mainly before birth, so it is not boosted after adolescence.

questions.stem: Which outcome is most associated with a severely deprived early environment, lacking stimulation, language and affection?
options: Delays in cognitive, language and social development
Faster language development because of fewer distractions
Stronger attachments to caregivers later in life
No lasting effects once the child starts school
questions.explanation: Severe early deprivation is associated with delays in cognitive, language and social and emotional development, which may be lasting. Lack of stimulation does not speed up language.

questions.stem: Genie, the 'wild child', was discovered in Los Angeles in 1970 at about age 13. What had she experienced?
options: A happy childhood followed by a brain injury in her teens
Being raised by wild animals in a forest from early infancy onwards
Normal care, but in a family that spoke two different languages at home
Years of extreme isolation, with almost no language or social contact
questions.explanation: Genie had been kept in severe isolation for most of her childhood, with almost no exposure to language or social interaction. When found, she could barely speak.

questions.stem: After years of support, Genie learned many words but never fully mastered grammar. What does her case suggest?
options: Grammar is learned before vocabulary in normal development
Deprivation affects physical development but not language
There may be a critical or sensitive period for language development
Language develops normally at any age, as long as there is enough teaching
questions.explanation: Genie's limited grammar despite later teaching is often taken as evidence of a critical or sensitive period for language. If language developed normally at any age, she would have mastered grammar with enough support.

questions.stem: Why is it difficult to draw firm conclusions about development from Genie's case?
options: Genie was studied for too short a time for any language learning to be recorded
Too many children with very similar histories were studied at the same time
Her case was an experiment in which researchers controlled the length of her isolation
It is a single case, and it is unclear whether she had problems before her isolation
questions.explanation: One case may not generalise, and because her early history is unclear, researchers cannot rule out a pre-existing problem as a cause of her difficulties. Her isolation was abuse by her family, not an experiment.
